concept.name: Term factor
concept.definition: One of the two bond-market factors in Fama and French (1993), capturing maturity risk: TERM is the difference between the return on long-term government bonds and the return on short-term risk-free instruments (the one-month Treasury bill rate), proxying the term premium for bearing interest-rate risk.
concept.intuition: Long bonds swing more when rates move, and investors historically demanded extra return for that - TERM measures that extra return month by month.
concept.mechanics: Constructed as the total return of a long-term government bond index minus a short-term risk-free rate (e.g., 1-month T-bill); bond and stock returns load on TERM to the extent they are exposed to shifts in the term structure of interest rates.
concept.formula: TERM_t = R_LTG,t - R_f,t, where R_LTG is the return on long-term government bonds and R_f the one-month T-bill rate.
concept.failure_modes: TERM captures exposure only to roughly parallel rate moves; non-parallel yield-curve shifts (steepeners, flatteners) leave residual risk, and the term premium itself varies over time and has been compressed or negative in some eras.
concept.misconceptions: TERM is not the level or slope of the yield curve: it is a realized return spread between long government bonds and bills, which differs from the ex-ante term premium embedded in forward rates.
concept.example: If the long-term Treasury index returns 1.5% in a month when T-bills return 0.4%, TERM realizes +1.1%; a bond fund with high duration will show high sensitivity to this factor.

citations.source: Bektic, Wenzler, Wegener, Schiereck, and Spielmann, Extending Fama-French Factors to Corporate Bond Markets (working paper, describing the Fama-French 1993 TERM and DEF factors)
